question: Name the most important HTTP security response headers and what each does.
answer:
- Strict-Transport-Security (HSTS): tells browsers to use HTTPS only for this domain for a stated max-age. Eliminates downgrade attacks and protocol-rollback.
- Content-Security-Policy (CSP): restricts which sources of script/style/etc. can load on the page. Primary defense against XSS at the browser layer.
- X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff: prevents the browser from guessing a different MIME type than the server sent. Stops one class of "upload a 'JPEG' that's actually a script" attacks.
- X-Frame-Options: DENY (or CSP frame-ancestors 'none'): prevents your page from being framed by another site. Defense against clickjacking. CSP frame-ancestors replaces this in modern browsers.
- Referrer-Policy: controls what the browser sends in the Referer header. strict-origin-when-cross-origin is a sensible default.
- Permissions-Policy (formerly Feature-Policy): restricts which powerful browser features (camera, mic, geolocation, USB, payment) can be used on the page or in iframes.
- Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy (COOP), Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy (COEP), Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy (CORP): isolate the browsing context so cross-origin scripts can't reach into your window or read your resources. Required to use SharedArrayBuffer or high-resolution timers.
- Cache-Control / Pragma on sensitive responses: no-store on logged-in pages and API responses prevents disk/CDN caching of private data.

Notable headers that are NOT useful anymore:
- X-XSS-Protection: legacy, IE/old-Chrome only, deprecated. Either set 0 or omit.
- Public-Key-Pins (HPKP): deprecated, dangerous, removed from browsers.

question: What does HSTS do exactly, and what's the role of the preload list?
answer:
HSTS (HTTP Strict Transport Security) tells the browser: "for this domain, never use plain HTTP. If a user types example.com or clicks an http:// link, rewrite to https://. If the certificate is invalid, refuse outright — no warning bypass." The directive: Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=63072000; includeSubDomains; preload.

- max-age: how long the browser caches this rule (commonly 1-2 years).
- includeSubDomains: applies the rule to every subdomain. Make sure all subdomains can really serve HTTPS before adding this — otherwise you've just broken them.
- preload: opt-in indicator for the browser preload list.

The preload list (hstspreload.org) is a list shipped inside major browsers themselves. Domains on it are treated as HSTS-protected from the user's very first visit — eliminating the "first-request bootstrap problem" where the very first HTTP request could be MitM'd before the HSTS header was ever seen.

Caveat: getting on the preload list is essentially permanent. Removal can take months and propagation takes browser releases. Don't preload a domain you might want to serve over HTTP again.

question: What's the difference between X-Frame-Options and CSP frame-ancestors?
answer:
Both control whether your page can be embedded in a frame on another origin — the primary defense against clickjacking.

X-Frame-Options is the older mechanism: a single header with three valid values — DENY (no framing), SAMEORIGIN (only same-origin), and ALLOW-FROM uri (any framing source — rarely supported and deprecated).

CSP frame-ancestors is the modern replacement: frame-ancestors 'self' is the equivalent of SAMEORIGIN; frame-ancestors 'none' is DENY; frame-ancestors can list multiple specific origins; supports wildcards and protocol restrictions.

Differences in practice:
- frame-ancestors supports multiple allowed origins; X-Frame-Options can't list multiples.
- frame-ancestors integrates with CSP reporting, so violation attempts can be observed.
- All modern browsers honor frame-ancestors; older ones may only honor X-Frame-Options.
- If both are present, frame-ancestors wins where supported.

Recommended practice: set both for maximum coverage. X-Frame-Options: DENY plus Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'none' — same intent, broadest support.

For pages that legitimately need to be framed (e.g., embeddable widgets), frame-ancestors is the only tool flexible enough to express "frame me only on partner-x.com and partner-y.com."

question: What is Referrer-Policy and what value would you choose for a typical app?
answer:
Referrer-Policy controls what the browser puts in the Referer header on outbound requests (links, image loads, script fetches, fetch/XHR). The Referer header can leak sensitive information — URLs may contain session tokens, search queries, internal paths, or user IDs.

Values, from most permissive to most restrictive:
- unsafe-url: always send the full URL including path and query. Bad — leaks freely.
- no-referrer-when-downgrade: full URL when going http->http or https->https, nothing when downgrading. Old default.
- strict-origin-when-cross-origin: full URL on same-origin requests; origin only on cross-origin same-scheme requests; nothing on downgrade. This is the modern default and a sensible choice for most apps.
- same-origin: full URL on same-origin requests; nothing cross-origin.
- strict-origin: origin only (no path/query) on same-scheme requests; nothing on downgrade.
- origin: send the origin (no path/query) always.
- no-referrer: send nothing, ever. Strongest privacy; can break some referer-based analytics and CSRF heuristics.

Typical recommendation: strict-origin-when-cross-origin. It preserves useful debugging on internal navigation, leaks only the origin to third parties, and blocks leakage on http downgrades.

For sensitive pages (password reset, payment, internal dashboards), tighten to no-referrer or strict-origin to minimize leakage of URLs that may contain tokens or identifiers.

Note: don't put secrets in URLs in the first place. Referrer-Policy is a mitigation, not a fix for URL-based secret leakage.

question: Walk through a hardened baseline of headers you'd ship for a new production web app.
answer:
A reasonable baseline (set globally; override per-route as needed):

Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=63072000; includeSubDomains; preload
- 2 years; covers subdomains; eligible for preload after submission.

Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'none'; script-src 'nonce-XYZ' 'strict-dynamic'; style-src 'self' 'nonce-XYZ'; img-src 'self' data: https:; font-src 'self'; connect-src 'self' https://api.example.com; frame-ancestors 'self'; base-uri 'self'; form-action 'self'; object-src 'none'; require-trusted-types-for 'script'; report-to csp-endpoint
- Strict, nonce-based, includes Trusted Types, modern best practice.

X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff
- Disable MIME sniffing.

X-Frame-Options: DENY
- Belt-and-braces with frame-ancestors above.

Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin
- Sensible default.

Permissions-Policy: accelerometer=(), camera=(), geolocation=(), gyroscope=(), microphone=(), payment=(), usb=()
- Lock down powerful features unless you actually need them; allowlist origins for ones you do.

Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin
Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp (if you need cross-origin isolation for SharedArrayBuffer)
Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy: same-origin (on resource responses, not pages)
- Isolation against Spectre-class side channels.

Cache-Control: no-store on authenticated HTML and JSON responses; max-age=31536000, immutable on hashed static assets.

Server / X-Powered-By / X-AspNet-Version: omit. Fingerprinting helps nobody but attackers.

Report-To / Reporting-Endpoints: configure a reports endpoint so CSP / network-error / deprecation reports flow somewhere you'll see them.

Deployment notes:
- Test the CSP in report-only mode first to catch legitimate violations.
- Don't preload HSTS until you've verified every subdomain serves HTTPS correctly.
- Tier the headers by route group — login/checkout get stricter Referrer-Policy and Cache-Control than the marketing site.
- Make the headers config-driven, so security team can adjust without a redeploy.

question: How do you measure and monitor security-header coverage across a large fleet of services?
answer:
Goal: every public endpoint emits the right headers consistently, and regressions are detected fast.

1. Centralize header policy: don't let every service implement its own. Put security headers in a shared middleware, edge proxy (nginx, Envoy), or CDN (Cloudflare, Fastly) so a single change propagates everywhere. Treat header config as code.

2. Inventory the surface area: maintain a list of every host/route exposed publicly. Tools: service registry, ingress configs, DNS scrape. The exercise itself usually surfaces forgotten endpoints.

3. Continuous scanning: a CI job (or scheduled batch) runs against every public endpoint and checks for the required headers. Tools: securityheaders.com API, OWASP ZAP, custom scripts using curl + jq. Fail builds when a service regresses; report deltas to a dashboard.

4. CSP violation reports: configure a report endpoint and ship reports into your log pipeline. Dashboard them by app, by directive, by blocked-uri. Spikes mean: real attempted XSS, broken third-party integration, or a code change that broke the policy.

5. HSTS preload tracker: alert on any expired/lowered HSTS header, since rollback risk is high.

6. Cert / TLS health: HSTS is only useful if HTTPS is solid. Monitor certificate expiry, weak ciphers, and protocol versions per host. Tools: Mozilla Observatory, Qualys SSL Labs, internal scanners.

7. Differential measurement: bucket findings by service, team, and severity. Publish a leaderboard. Social pressure works.

8. Tier-of-coverage SLOs: 99% of services emit HSTS; 95% emit a non-trivial CSP; 80% emit Trusted Types. Track over time. Trend lines are more motivating than a binary fail.

9. Onboarding new services: every new service template includes the standard middleware. The default path is the safe path; opting out requires explicit override.

10. Pen-test feedback: every pen-test finding tied to a missing header becomes a regression test and a coverage gap to close.

11. Customer-facing reports: for B2B SaaS, customers increasingly ask for security headers reports as part of vendor security review. Having them in good shape is both protection and revenue.

Failure modes to watch for:
- Header dropped at a downstream proxy (compression, caching layer).
- Headers different on cached vs origin responses.
- Per-route overrides drifting (login page is hardened, signup is not).
- Subdomains forgotten — security headers focus on www but api.example.com is naked.
